Hi Karthik / Lauren,

We're kicking off the private deployment for Redwood in our AWS environment and need guidance on which connectivity pattern to adopt: VPC Peering, AWS PrivateLink (endpoint services), or a site-to-site (S2S) VPN into our Transit VPC. Our constraints:

- Multi-account AWS org (separate account per environment).
- Central transit/account hub for shared services and egress inspection appliances.
- Must satisfy HIPAA controls (no public exposure of PHI; auditability).
- Expect moderate data transfer (daily batch syncs of large datasets) + low-latency inference traffic for clinical UI.
- Timeline: pilot environment in 3 weeks; production in 10-12 weeks.

Attached is a simple network diagram to illustrate current layout. Can you provide a short recommendation and a risk/cost matrix? Also need to know whether PrivateLink can be routed through our inspection appliances (we depend on inline inspection for egress).

Anna — thanks for the clear brief and diagram. High level: we typically recommend a hybrid pattern depending on traffic profile: PrivateLink for control/API planes (secure, cross-account, no route table changes), and either Transit Gateway or S2S for large, bulk data movement where cost per GB and bandwidth matter. VPC Peering is great for low-latency intra-account traffic but scales poorly for many VPCs and can be awkward with central egress appliances.

I've attached a one-sheet comparison (connectivity-comparison-matrix.xlsx) that lays out pros/cons, security implications, and rough cost buckets. Lauren will add technical specifics and a proposed config.

On Sun, Aug 22, 2026 at 9:12 AM Anna Lim <anna.lim@holomed.com> wrote:
> We're kicking off the private deployment for Redwood in our AWS environment and need guidance on which connectivity pattern to adopt...

Hi Anna — following up with an engineering-focused comparison and a practical recommendation for pilot vs production. TL;DR: For your constraints (multi-account + central egress inspection + HIPAA):

- Recommendation (pilot): S2S VPN into a dedicated Redwood customer VPC attached to your Transit Gateway.
  - Why: fastest to stand up, preserves your inspection path, minimal IAM changes, good for validating app behavior.
  - Drawbacks: higher latency, lower bandwidth ceiling, operational overhead (IPsec management).

- Recommendation (production): Hybrid — PrivateLink for control/API endpoints (model inference endpoints and management API) + Transit Gateway (or TGW attachments) for bulk dataset transfers and on-prem synchronization.
  - PrivateLink pros: cross-account, no route table peering, endpoint services are reachable via ENIs in your VPC, simplifies least-privilege exposure.
  - PrivateLink cons: traffic to PrivateLink endpoints does not traverse customer route tables in the way peered VPC traffic does; you can NAT/forward from your VPC to inspection appliances but that requires explicit construction (e.g., route traffic from endpoint ENIs through an inspection subnet using proxy/NLB design).

- VPC Peering: consider only if both parties are in the same AWS account or a very small number (<3) of VPCs; it gives low-latency, full L3 reachability but has no concept of transitive routing (so it will not traverse your TGW/inspection appliances automatically).

Risk / Feature matrix (short):
- Egress inspection: Transit Gateway or S2S preserves in-path appliances; PrivateLink needs explicit proxying or a partner NLB-based design.
- Cross-account complexity: PrivateLink wins for security boundaries.
- Bandwidth/cost: Peering/TGW cheaper per-GB than PrivateLink for sustained large transfers; PrivateLink incurs endpoint and data processing charges.
- Latency: Peering < PrivateLink < S2S (approx).
- Scalability: TGW > PrivateLink (endpoint services per-region limits) > Peering (N^2).

Example configs / notes:
- If you require all traffic to go through an inline inspection appliance: prefer TGW with a flow-log/route table that steers traffic through an inspection VPC. For PrivateLink-based API traffic, deploy a proxy in the customer's VPC that forwards to the endpoint and routes through inspection appliances.
- Authentication: PrivateLink + mutual TLS on the endpoint is an effective control for HIPAA data plane.

Next steps:
1) Confirm pilot scope (inference-only vs inference+bulk sync).
2) If pilot includes bulk sync, we stand up an S2S VPN attached to your Transit Gateway.
3) We'll provide a prescriptive runbook for the PrivateLink proxy pattern if you want the production path to include PrivateLink.

Available times for call: Thu 8/26 10–11am PT (Karthik suggested) — happy to take a deep dive and sketch the route tables.

Anna — quick engineering note to add to Lauren's excellent writeup:

- PrivateLink behavior: endpoint services create ENIs in the consumer VPC. Those ENIs are routable IPs in your VPC; you can route traffic from those ENIs to an inspection appliance, but you cannot change how AWS manages the endpoint's ENI-to-VP C path (i.e., the endpoint is owned by AWS). The practical pattern we use: create an internal NLB in Redwood account fronting the service, accept PrivateLink connections, and provide a small proxy (in your VPC or ours) that forwards to the NLB. To ensure inspection, you place the proxy behind your inspection subnets or route proxy egress through the Transit GW.

- Hybrid recommendation (for procurement):
  1) Pilot: S2S VPN -> TGW (attaches to your Transit VPC) for bulk data and to validate inspection.
  2) Production: PrivateLink for API/ingress (mutual TLS + endpoint policies) + TGW for bulk transfers. This reduces blast radius and keeps PHI out of public endpoints.

- Cost note: PrivateLink has a per-hour endpoint charge and per-GB processing. TGW/S2S has hourly attachment + data transfer. For your projected daily syncs, TGW + S2S will likely be cheaper for sustained transfers; PrivateLink is more predictable for control traffic. We'll provide a cost estimate in the next update.

I'll attach a short SOW and a draft runbook for the proxy pattern. Proposed call: Thu 8/26 10am PT — confirm and we'll send the calendar invite.
